idiom_name: subject query operation (getExtension) + extension objects keyed by an identifier, with an optional adapter registry
implementation_notes: Give the subject one extra operation that takes an extension identifier and returns either an object implementing the requested extension interface or an empty answer (null, nil, None, false) - never an exception, because absence is a normal outcome. Keep every extension interface separate from the base interface and let the extension object (not necessarily the subject) implement it, so extensions can adapt foreign types. Identify extensions by a type object where the language has one (Class, typeid, TypeId, Protocol, symbol) and by a namespaced, registry-checked name only where it does not. Add an adapter factory or registry keyed by subject type when extensions must be supplied for classes that cannot be edited, cache per-subject extension objects and state who releases them. Clients must treat every capability as optional: probe once, then take a degraded path instead of failing.
pitfalls: The query must never throw or abort: absence is a normal answer and callers must be able to continue without the extension.
Extensions attached to a subject need an ownership rule; a fresh adapter per query leaks or churns, and one cached extension per subject must be released with it.
Identifier discipline: without a single registry (type objects where possible, namespaced names otherwise) two extensions collide and the lookup silently answers with the wrong interface.
A capability that every caller needs must not be modelled as an extension; it belongs in the base interface or in a required parameter.
Probing by dynamic cast or reflection in a hot loop defeats the purpose - resolve once where the capability set is not genuinely dynamic.

Wrong move: branch on which extension a received object supports inside shared code (if x is Dog fetch, else if x is Bird fly) -> the function silently binds to today's subtype set, every new extension forces edits at every probe site, and a missed branch surfaces as a run-time type error -> instead keep behaviour in the polymorphic dispatch (a base-interface default) or declare the capability a required parameter.

Wrong move: ask a wrapper for its type identity to locate the payload's extension (calling type_id() on a Box<dyn Any> in Rust) -> it answers with the container's identity, every downcast misses, and the probe silently degrades to the fallback path -> instead coerce to the inner trait object (&*boxed) before querying and centralise that unwrap in one adapter.

Wrong move: invent polymorphic identifiers so one element answers to both a base key and a derived key -> subtype lookups resolve unpredictably, and the design is error-prone enough that Kotlin deprecated polymorphic CoroutineContext keys (AbstractCoroutineContextKey) in 2.4 -> instead query by the base key and cast explicitly at one site, or expose a dedicated accessor per element type.
